*INTERNAL NOTE - SUMMARY OF ANALYSIS* 

I have considered Debbie’s questions and carried out a risk analysis. 

+Background and latest developments+

* Ops proposes launching a *child seat category* in London (likely on Scheduled Rides first), with possible later expansion to Rest of UK (2026).
* [~accountid:5d8df399c7d4e30dc2836580] has confirmed that Insurance have not raised any issues, however CO to check this point. 
* Proposed launching with booster seats initially (which I agree with, if we launch - easier for drivers to fit, more affordable etc). 

+Key Risks/Considerations+ 

* *Safety & Liability:* My biggest concern is around safety, especially as this involves children. Risks include: injury from wrong seat size, defective seat, improper installation, an accident involving child. 
* *Reputation/Media Backlash:* this risk is heightened due to child safety focus if an incident were to be reported in the media*.* 
* *Reclassification:* if we provide the seats ourselves, there is risk with providing equipment that must be used to fulfil services. That being said, providing seats ourselves (that we have properly vetted and inspected) potentially outweighs the risk of drivers sourcing their own seats which may be defective or poor quality. 
* *Post-incident claim that Bolt supplied unsafe/defective seat:* If we provide the seats ourselves, we are potentially liable (or at least perceived to be liable) in the event of improper installation/passenger complaint etc.
* *Passenger complaints:* passengers could argue that they have been misled to believe that the child seat category is suitable for all children (this is where disclaimers and clear t&cs are important). 

+Mitigations+

* engage the PR team for their stance. 
* run full business case review - at this stage, I am not clear on what the revenue forecast is / what the benefits of launching are / what the expected uptake among drivers and passengers is. [~accountid:5d8df399c7d4e30dc2836580] is keen to launch something that Uber hasn’t launched in the UK and I appreciate the competitive edge angle. However, it is important to consider the reasons why Uber has not launched this category. 

*NEXT STEPS*

* [~accountid:612f31d89976c300693ebaf7] has provided initial thoughts in [this sub-ticket|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-53439]. CO to check whether Global Passenger T&Cs will incorporate any updates re child safety/child seat categories. 
* potentially loop PR in / have a further discussion with [~accountid:5d8df399c7d4e30dc2836580].

Dear Liis,

 

Thank you for sharing your standard Data Processing Agreement (DPA) and for your detailed explanation of the reasoning behind it. We have reviewed the document carefully.

 

Unfortunately, we are unable to proceed with your standard DPA in its current form. The main reason is that it does not reflect the dual role that City Legal Solicitors plays in this engagement. While we do act as a processor for certain data (such as data processed through our portal services), we also act as a controller in other instances for example, when determining retention periods for client files, reporting to UK authorities, and fulfilling our professional and regulatory obligations. Giving you an update on this case

*Material Law (The Crime)*
The investigation concerns Section 279 of the Danish Criminal Code, which defines the crime of fraud. This section only defines the offence; *it does not provide a legal basis for data disclosure.*

*Procedural Law (Police Powers)*
The *Danish Administration of Justice Act (Retsplejeloven)* outlines the police’s authority to request information during an investigation.
This act explains what the police are empowered to do and request.
The specific power to compel a third party to disclose information typically requires a court order under *Section 804(1) of this act.*
---
*Although the police did not cite Section 804(1) in their request, we can reasonably assume it is the legal basis for their operations. We can proceed with responding to this request. However, for future reference, we should encourage them to cite the specific legal provision from the Administration of Justice Act to ensure clarity.*

For the audit trail, below is the list of aggregated factors the privacy team documented to demonstrate that NZ riders would reasonably expect Flamingo partner offers under a soft opt-in (implied consent) model:

#* Both Bolt (ride-hailing) and Flamingo (electric scooter rentals) operate within the same urban mobility ecosystem. Users booking rides through Bolt could be expected to view micro-mobility services as a complementary part of their journey—so it is reasonable for them to expect offers that bridge the two, such as Flamingo credit to extend or connect their point-to-point travel.
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
As discussed, the local regulator may challenge Bolt’s stance, especially since:

* the campaign does not distinguish between users who have merely registered in the app and those who have previously taken rides.
* Bolt did not validate its assumptions about user expectations.
